newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China corn crop seen at record, plenty for export.
newsitem.headline: China corn crop seen at record, plenty for export.

text.p: China is heading for a record corn crop this year and will have plenty left over for export if the government lifts a long-term ban on selling the grain overseas, traders and diplomats said on Thursday.
The corn crop under harvest in the far northeast looks set to be between 115 and 120 million tonnes, said grain industry sources just returned from a tour of the region.
Farmers in Heilongjiang and Jilin provinces were happy with increased yields. The weather had been good and acreage had increased over 1995, the sources said.
Last year's corn crop was a record 112 million tonnes, and "this year is certainly going to be a couple of million tonnes higher than that," a U.S. marketing executive said.

The prospect of China once again becoming a corn exporter was shot down earlier on Thursday by an official of China's National Maize Export Co, who told Reuters that Beijing was not preparing to lift its December 1994 ban on corn exports.
Before then, China had been one of the world's biggest corn sellers. It exported 10 million tonnes in 1994.

Customs figures show just 120,000 tonnes of corn were exported in the first eight months of 1996, mostly to Japan and South Korea, but officials said the deals were exceptional and not an indication that the ban had been lifted.
Heilongjiang, Jilin and Liaoning provinces in the far northeast are China's major corn producers. Corn is also grown in Shandong, Hebei and Henan provinces.

An industry source just returned from a tour of cropland in Heilongjiang and Jilin told Reuters that agriculture and grain officials in each province were expecting output to be up at least two million tonnes on last year's crop.
Heilongjiang's corn crop should go from the 12.2 million tonnes harvested in 1995, to between 14 and 15 million, he said.
In Jilin, the corn production should be 17.1 million tonnes, after last year's 14.98 million tonnes, he said.
The new crop could be stored without too many logistical headaches, despite the large amounts currently stored in the northeast, traders said.

Traders have said about two million tonnes of corn is stored at Dalian, having been moved there in April and May in anticipation of exports being allowed to boost prices that fell in some northern areas to below 1,000 yuan ($120) a tonne.
Fear of fuelling inflation and the possiblity of future grain tightness were said to be behind a top government decision to maintain the export ban.
But while the ban remained, provincial grain bureaux that bought corn in the hope of profiting on exports were losing enormous amounts of money on storage and interest on loans.
China's provincial grain bureaux purchase 20 percent of the crop at a fixed procurement price, which last year was between 660 and 700 yuan per tonne. This grain goes to central reserves.
Another 40 percent is commercial grain, which the grain bureaux buy at double the procurement rate.
The grain bureaux often take out bank loans in order to purchase the commerical grain, but are not permitted to hedge.
"This is where the problems come up," said a diplomatic source. "When the market crashes, like corn did last year, they have no way to hedge so they get burned."
Loans added 15 percent to the cost of the corn, he said.
"What incentives do the bureaux have? It is not their money," he said.

"There are huge loans for these purchases that are not performing. So do they cut their losses and export and clear their inventories -- assuming exports are permitted? Or do they keep hanging on and hoping for higher prices?
"In the light of new crop figures, I don't think prices will be moving up any time soon," he said.
